# AI Agent Memory Systems: Comparative Survey 2025–2026

## The Benchmark Landscape — What's Actually Measurable

Three evaluation datasets dominate the space in 2025–2026:

- **LoCoMo** (ECAI 2025): 35 sessions, 300+ turns; tests factual recall over long multi-session histories.
- **LongMemEval**: 500 single-session questions; preferred by several vendors for its harder temporal-reasoning demands.
- **MemoryArena** (arXiv:2602.16313, Stanford/UCSD, submitted for ICML 2026): the most credible *independent* benchmark — systems scoring 85–94% on LoCoMo "plummet to 40–60%" on MemoryArena's interdependent multi-session tasks. This gap is the most important signal in the field.

**Critical caveat on all vendor scores below**: there is no neutral leaderboard. Every score except Chronos (PwC arXiv paper, independently peer-reviewed at [arxiv.org/abs/2603.16862](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.16862)) is a vendor self-report on public data — reproducible in principle, not audited in practice.

---

## System-by-System Summary

### Mem0
Architecture: multi-signal hybrid (vector + entity graph + user/session/agent scoping). April 2026 algorithm uses single-pass hierarchical extraction. Self-reported: ~91.6% LoCoMo, ~94.8% LongMemEval (inconsistent between sources; treat as directionally ~90–95%). Earlier 2025 figures were 66.9% LoCoMo / 0.71s latency vs full-context 72.9% / 9.87s. Production integrations: 13 agent frameworks, 20 vector stores. Managed SaaS + open-source.
Sources: [mem0.ai/blog/state-of-ai-agent-memory-2026](https://mem0.ai/blog/state-of-ai-agent-memory-2026), [agentry.press](https://agentry.press/news/mem0-algorithm-update-hits-91-6-on-locomo-94-8-on-longmemeval/)

**Memory tiers**: implements working (run/session), episodic (user_id across sessions), semantic (entity extraction + deduplication), and organizational (app_id/org_id) scopes. No explicit procedural memory.

### Zep / Graphiti
Architecture: temporal knowledge graph with bi-temporal modeling (creation + expiration timestamps on edges). Graphiti preserves the *evolution* of facts rather than replacing them. Self-reported: 94.7% LoCoMo, 90.2% LongMemEval on their own product page — but Zep has a documented history of contested benchmark claims (Mem0 counter-claimed 58.44% in a prior dispute). Treat these numbers with skepticism.
Sources: [getzep.com/platform/graphiti](https://www.getzep.com/platform/graphiti)

**Memory tiers**: semantic (graph entities/relations), episodic (timestamped facts with validity windows), working (thread context). No procedural.

### Letta (formerly MemGPT)
Architecture: OS-paging model — main context (working memory), recall database (episodic), archival vector store (semantic). Explicit memory block abstraction gives agents direct control over what stays in context. Self-reported LoCoMo ~83%; MemoryOS variant incurred 32.4s user-facing latency in the arXiv:2602.19320 empirical study — highest of any tested system.
Sources: [Anatomy of Agentic Memory, arXiv:2602.19320](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.19320v1)

**Memory tiers**: working / episodic / semantic (all three explicit). The OS metaphor is the closest to a classical cognitive model.

### LangMem (LangChain/LangGraph)
Architecture: LangGraph-native SDK. Uses `trustcall` for type-safe consolidation and invalidation. Explicitly supports semantic (grounding facts), procedural (prompt instructions updated via metaprompt reflection/gradient critique), and episodic (few-shot examples) — though the docs note episodic utilities are not yet fully built out. The consolidation loop prevents memory hoarding by balancing creation vs. invalidation. No benchmark scores published.
Sources: [langchain.com/blog/langmem-sdk-launch](https://www.langchain.com/blog/langmem-sdk-launch), [langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/concepts/conceptual_guide](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langmem/concepts/conceptual_guide/)

**Memory tiers**: all three classic types named explicitly; procedural (updated system prompts) is the most distinctive feature.

### Cognee
Architecture: six-stage pipeline — classify → permissions → chunk → entity/relationship extraction → summarize → embed + graph commit. Self-improving: prunes stale nodes, strengthens frequent connections, reweights edges based on usage signals (September 2025 memify layer). Raised $7.5M seed (Pebblebed, cofounders of OpenAI/FAIR) February 2026. 500x growth in pipeline runs in 2025 (~1M+ runs).
Sources: [github.com/topoteretes/cognee](https://github.com/topoteretes/cognee), [cognee.ai/blog/cognee-news/cognee-raises-seven-million-five-hundred-thousand-dollars-seed](https://www.cognee.ai/blog/cognee-news/cognee-raises-seven-million-five-hundred-thousand-dollars-seed)

**Memory tiers**: semantic (graph + vector), episodic (self-improving edges), no explicit procedural.

### A-MEM (NeurIPS 2025)
**Peer-reviewed** (NeurIPS 2025, OpenReview: [openreview.net/forum?id=FiM0M8gcct](https://openreview.net/forum?id=FiM0M8gcct)). Zettelkasten-style interconnected note network — new memories trigger contextual updates to existing notes (keywords, tags, relation links). Token reduction vs LoCoMo/MemGPT baselines: 85–93% (from ~16,900 to ~1,200–2,500 tokens per query). Retrieval: 3.70µs at 1M in-memory notes. Most credible performance numbers of any open-source system.
Sources: [arxiv.org/abs/2502.12110](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12110)

**Memory tiers**: unified entity-centric model; closest to semantic + episodic in one structure.

### Memobase
Architecture: user-profile-first — structures memory into demographic, interest, and psychological trait categories rather than raw facts. Caps LLM calls at 3 per run (~40–50% token reduction). Sub-100ms retrieval via SQL on structured profiles. MCP-native. Positioned for personalization use cases, not agent task memory.
Sources: [github.com/memodb-io/memobase](https://github.com/memodb-io/memobase)

**Memory tiers**: semantic profile (structured user model) + episodic event timeline. No working or procedural.

### MemOS
Architecture: four-layer model (L1 Traces → L2 Policies → L3 World Model → Crystallized Skills), with multi-modal support (text, images, tools), natural-language memory feedback, async ingestion via MemScheduler. Claims: 43.70% accuracy vs OpenAI Memory, 35.24% token savings, 40.43% on LongMemEval. These are **author self-reported in an unreviewed arXiv preprint** (arXiv:2507.03724) with no disclosed methodology for the baseline comparisons — treat as marketing until independently replicated.
Sources: [github.com/MemTensor/MemOS](https://github.com/MemTensor/MemOS)

**Memory tiers**: closest system to explicit procedural memory ("Crystallized Skills" tier for cross-task skill reuse).

---

## OpenAI and Anthropic

**OpenAI Dreaming V3** (launched June 4, 2026): background "dreaming" synthesizes memories from chat history automatically rather than requiring explicit saves. Internal eval progression (OpenAI-only benchmark, undisclosed dataset): factual recall 41.5% (2024) → 67.9% (2025) → 82.8% (2026); time-sensitive accuracy 9.4% → 52.2% → 75.1%. Free-tier rollout. No external validation.
Sources: [openai.com/index/chatgpt-memory-dreaming](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-memory-dreaming)

**Anthropic Claude Memory Tool** (beta, launched September 2025): file-based CRUD over a `/memories` directory — Markdown/structured files, no vector DB, just-in-time retrieval. Client-side controlled: the application executes all memory operations and owns storage. Upcoming "File Memory" mode distributes notes across topic/project-organized documents vs. the current "Classic" single-file mode. Design principle: favors auditability and developer control over opaque embedding stores.
Sources: [platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool)

---

## Emerging Systems and Patterns

**New entrants clearly gaining traction in 2026:**
- **Hindsight** (Vectorize): consolidation-focused system; operates a vendor-run "Agent Memory Benchmark" at agentmemorybenchmark.ai (conflict of interest noted). Best-documented consolidation design in the field. [hindsight.vectorize.io/blog/2026/05/21/agent-memory-consolidation](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/blog/2026/05/21/agent-memory-consolidation)
- **Chronos** (PwC): best independently-verified score at 95.60% on LongMemEval-S using Claude Opus. [arxiv.org/abs/2603.16862](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.16862)
- **EverMind EverOS**: "memory operating system" with multimodal ingestion, self-evolution via Cases/Skills; eval data public on GitHub but unverified by third parties. [evermind.ai/blogs/best-open-source-agent-memory-frameworks-2026](https://evermind.ai/blogs/best-open-source-agent-memory-frameworks-2026)
- **Graphiti** (standalone, also underpins Zep): bi-temporal graphs for tracking fact validity windows.
- **AWS Bedrock AgentCore Memory**: managed memory layer that integrates with LangGraph and other frameworks. [docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/memory-integrate-lang.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/memory-integrate-lang.html)

**Structural shift**: the category has fractured. Vendors now specialize: Memobase → user personalization; Mem0 → general-purpose production layer; Zep/Graphiti → temporal reasoning; LangMem → LangGraph-native procedural; MemOS → multi-modal + skill reuse; Cognee → organizational knowledge graph.

**ICLR 2026 MemAgents workshop** (independently verified, Rio de Janeiro): 110+ submissions, keynotes from Chelsea Finn and Jeff Clune. Signals the field has reached academic-conference critical mass. [iclr.cc/virtual/2026/workshop/10000792](https://iclr.cc/virtual/2026/workshop/10000792)

---

## Memory Tier Taxonomy (Academic Consensus)

The March 2026 survey [arXiv:2603.07670](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.07670v1) formalizes four tiers with a write–manage–read loop as the unifying model:

| Tier | What it stores | Key challenge |
|------|---------------|---------------|
| **Working memory** | Current context window | Compression without drift |
| **Episodic memory** | Timestamped concrete experiences | Staleness when user circumstances change |
| **Semantic memory** | Abstracted de-contextualized facts | Deduplication, contradiction resolution |
| **Procedural memory** | Reusable skills, updated instructions | Learning from failure without entrenchment |

The [arXiv:2602.19320 empirical study](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.19320v1) found that MemoryOS (Letta-style) incurred 32.4s latency due to hierarchical paging while SimpleMem hit 1.06s — showing working memory tier management has severe latency costs if done naively.

---

## Write-Path and Consolidation Quality

The highest-signal technical piece on this is the Hindsight blog's Four Levers framework ([hindsight.vectorize.io/blog/2026/05/21/agent-memory-consolidation](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/blog/2026/05/21/agent-memory-consolidation)):

1. **Importance** — what gets written at all (LLM-rated scoring or fact extraction as filter)
2. **Merge** — entity resolution at write-time, deduplication, conflict policy (recency-wins vs. confidence-wins)
3. **Decay** — exponential confidence decay (Ebbinghaus curve); most systems skip this entirely
4. **Eviction** — primarily for compliance (GDPR), not performance

The arXiv:2603.07670 survey's key consolidation finding: systems oscillate between **hoarding** (noise drowns signal) and **amnesia** (low-frequency critical facts vanish). No system has principled consolidation. The recommended write-path order: fact-level extraction → entity resolution during writes → decay only for temporal state → eviction for compliance only.

The [TiMem paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.02845) (arXiv:2601.02845, Jan 2026) addresses staged write-path consolidation specifically for long-horizon agents: hot buffer with probation before promotion to long-term storage, mirroring hippocampal-to-neocortical transfer.

---

## Key Unsolved Problems (per Mem0's production gap analysis)

1. **Temporal abstraction at scale**: 25% performance drop going from 1M to 10M token contexts
2. **Cross-session structure**: most systems treat changes as replacement, not evolution
3. **Staleness**: high-relevance facts become "confidently wrong" when user circumstances change
4. **Cross-session identity**: unstable user IDs break with multi-device/anonymous sessions
5. **Privacy/consent**: retention, deletion, and access controls remain application-level decisions

The MemoryArena benchmark (arXiv:2602.16313) is the honest signal: the 40–60% scores there vs. 85–94% on LoCoMo reveal that headline benchmarks are optimistic relative to real agentic use.

---

**Mem0 write path and multi-writer safety — findings**

**Write timing: explicit API call, not automatic**
Memory extraction is triggered by explicit `memory.add(messages, user_id=...)` calls — the caller (your agent code) invokes it after each turn. There is no built-in per-turn hook, end-of-session flush, or background job. Common pattern: pipe last N messages into `add()` immediately after the assistant responds.

**Key API parameters:**
- `user_id` — long-term/user-scoped memory (most common)
- `agent_id` — AI persona-specific knowledge (agent-scoped)
- `run_id` — interaction thread / session context
- `messages` — conversation data to extract from
- `filters` — for scoped retrieval (e.g. `{"user_id": uid}`)

**Extraction pipeline (V3, April 2026):**
Single-pass LLM-powered fact extraction → ADD-only additive pipeline (no UPDATE/DELETE on extraction, which reduces write conflicts by design). Retrieval uses hybrid semantic + BM25 + entity matching.

**Multi-writer safety:**
- Concurrent reads: safe — multiple agents can call `search()` for same `user_id` simultaneously without conflict.
- Concurrent writes: serialized internally on Mem0 Cloud — two simultaneous `add()` calls for the same `user_id` queue rather than execute in parallel, preventing deduplication pipeline races.
- No explicit locking API exposed to callers.
- `AsyncMemory` / `AsyncMemoryClient` variants exist for async usage but concurrency guarantees are at the platform level, not documented as caller-controlled.
- Self-hosted: no documented serialization guarantees — concurrent writes to same user store could race depending on vector DB backend.

**Bottom line:** Write safety in multi-agent scenarios depends on whether you're on Mem0 Cloud (serialized) or self-hosted (backend-dependent, no documented guarantee). Scoping agents to separate `agent_id` or `run_id` namespaces reduces contention regardless.

- https://deepwiki.com/mem0ai/mem0

LangMem store topology and write path — findings:

**Store topology: single shared store**
One store instance (e.g., `InMemoryStore` or `AsyncPostgresStore`) passed to all agents via `store=` parameter. Not per-agent or per-session isolated — scoping is handled by namespace, not by separate stores.

Tuple-based, with template variables populated at runtime from `config["configurable"]`:

**Write path — two modes**
1. **Hot path (synchronous, per-turn):** Agent calls `create_manage_memory_tool(namespace=...)` during conversation. Agent decides to write before responding. Immediate, adds latency.
2. **Background (async):** `create_memory_store_manager("model", namespace=(...))` — invoked with `await memory_manager.ainvoke(to_process)`. Triggered per-message (each new message arrival) or deferred via "Delayed Memory Processing" to let conversation settle before extracting. No latency impact but memories not immediately available.

- `create_manage_memory_tool(namespace=...)` — hot-path write tool
- `create_search_memory_tool(namespace=...)` — read tool
- `create_memory_store_manager(model, namespace=...)` — background extractor
- `store.search(namespace, query=...)` — retrieval

LangMem technical findings (under 300 words):

**Memory Tiers**
LangMem does NOT use traditional working/core/archival tiers. It has two operational modes:
- **Hot-path**: Agent invokes memory tools directly during conversation (in-the-hot-path, blocking)
- **Background**: `ReflectionExecutor` defers and deduplicates memory processing after conversation ends (non-blocking)

Letta/MemGPT (a different framework) uses the 3-tier model: core memory (always in-context/RAM), archival memory (vector store/disk), recall memory (conversation history). Don't conflate with LangMem.

- `create_memory_manager()` — user-controlled, single LLM call for inserts/updates/deletes
- `create_memory_store_manager()` — auto-manages BaseStore (search, upserts, deletes)
- `create_manage_memory_tool(namespace)` — hot-path tool agents call directly
- `create_search_memory_tool(namespace)` — semantic retrieval tool
- `ReflectionExecutor` — background deferral + deduplication wrapper

- Agent-based mode (`create_react_agent`) gets multi-turn LLM calls for complex conflict handling vs. single-call mode for simple cases

**Hot-path vs Background**
- Hot-path: synchronous, in-conversation, agent-driven via tools
- Background: async via `ReflectionExecutor`, compatible with deduplication, runs post-conversation

<teammate-message teammate_id="search-mem0-consolidation" color="yellow" summary="Mem0 consolidation/dedup research findings">
**Mem0 Memory Consolidation & Dedup — Findings**

**AUDN Loop (core vector memory)**
Every incoming fact goes through a 4-operation decision cycle against the top-s semantically similar existing memories (retrieved by vector embedding):
- ADD — genuinely new information
- UPDATE — augments existing memory with newer/more detailed info
- DELETE — removes memories contradicted by new info
- NOOP — fact already exists or is irrelevant

The LLM makes this decision via function-calling, presented with both the candidate facts and the retrieved similar memories. This resolves contradictions before they accumulate rather than at retrieval time.

**Graph Memory (Mem0g) — conflict resolution**
Knowledge is stored as entity nodes + relationship triples: `(Subject) --[RELATIONSHIP]--> (Object)`. The graph pipeline uses a multi-stage LLM tool-calling flow:

1. Entity extraction via embedding + spaCy matching
2. Conflict Detector searches existing graph for contradicting relationships
3. LLM-based Update Resolver decides what to do — marks old relationships **invalid** rather than deleting them (preserves temporal reasoning)

Graph tools used by the LLM: `ADD_MEMORY_TOOL_GRAPH`, `UPDATE_MEMORY_TOOL_GRAPH`, `DELETE_MEMORY_TOOL_GRAPH`, `NOOP_TOOL`

**Key distinction**: Standard Mem0 DELETEs contradicted facts; Mem0g *invalidates* them (soft delete), so historical state is preserved for temporal queries.

**Retrieval fusion**: Hybrid — graph signals fused with semantic + BM25 scores.

**API params**: No explicit conflict/merge params documented publicly; the LLM prompt (`ADDITIVE_EXTRACTION_PROMPT`) and similarity-top-k (`top_s`) are the knobs. The platform tier has "Advanced Memory Operations" but params aren't in public docs.

**Sources**:
- https://memo.d.foundation/breakdown/mem0 (AUDN loop + graph tools detail)
- https://deepwiki.com/mem0ai/mem0/4.1-graph-memory-overview (graph pipeline)
- https://arxiv.org/html/2504.19413v1 (ECAI 2025 paper — BEAM benchmark, contradiction resolution category)
</teammate-message>

5. **[Mem0 Guide 2026 (RockB)](https://baeseokjae.github.io/posts/mem0-agent-memory-guide-2026/)**
   Third-party practical guide covering scoping patterns and retrieval composition.

## Key Findings

**Scoping model:** Mem0 uses four namespacing dimensions — `user_id`, `agent_id`, `run_id`, `app_id` (plus optional `org_id`). These are composed as filters at both write and retrieval time.

**How it works:**
- `user_id` → shared user facts that persist across all agents (preferences, history)
- `agent_id` → agent-isolated facts (prevents "billing agent seeing support tickets")
- `run_id` → session-level ephemeral context
- `app_id` → app-wide defaults

**Multi-agent sharing pattern:** The LlamaIndex cookbook shows agents sharing a single Mem0 instance but partitioned by `user_id`. All agents read/write to the same store; `user_id` is the logical isolation. `agent_id` is used for further per-agent isolation when needed.

**Write conflict prevention:** **Not handled by Mem0 itself.** The docs explicitly raise the question "What happens when two agents disagree about a fact?" without providing an automatic answer. The LlamaIndex example sidesteps this via orchestrator-enforced sequential writes (one agent writes at a time). There is no built-in locking, CAS, or conflict resolution — it's left to application architecture.

**Consolidation ownership:** Also application-level. Mem0's deduplication/consolidation runs as part of the `add()` pipeline (it merges new facts with existing ones via LLM), but when two agents write conflicting facts, there's no authoritative owner — last-write wins or the LLM merge picks one arbitrarily.

**Bottom line for SEVH/shared memory design:** Mem0's scoping is good for isolation but weak on concurrent writes. For a multi-agent swarm where agents write simultaneously, you need either (a) a single designated memory-writer agent, or (b) a message-queue/serialization layer in front of `mem0.add()`. The `agent_id` scope is clean for read isolation but doesn't prevent write races.

<teammate-message teammate_id="search-amem" color="blue" summary="A-MEM architecture research findings">
## A-MEM Architecture Research

**Correction on repo identity**: The repo is `WujiangXu/A-mem` (NeurIPS 2025 paper), not `qiaosenwang/a-mem` — that GitHub path returned 404. All findings below are from the correct repo and paper.

---

### Store Topology

**Single flat store per agent instance** — no per-session or per-agent-role isolation built in. Memories are kept in `self.memories` (a dict keyed by `note.id`) on the `AgenticMemorySystem` class. The retriever is a single vector index over all notes. The Zettelkasten-style design creates an interconnected knowledge graph within that flat store via `links` between `MemoryNote` objects, but there is no native multi-agent scoping or session partitioning in the code.

Source: https://github.com/WujiangXu/A-mem

---

### Write Path

**Synchronous, per-turn, on explicit `add_note()` call.** There is no background job, no end-of-session sweep, no automatic extraction. The caller is responsible for deciding what to write. The pipeline inside `add_note()`:

```python
def add_note(self, content: str, time: str = None, **kwargs) -> str:
    note = MemoryNote(content=content, llm_controller=self.llm_controller,
                      timestamp=time, **kwargs)
    evo_label, note = self.process_memory(note)       # LLM evolution step
    self.memories[note.id] = note
    self.retriever.add_documents([...combined metadata...])
    if evo_label and self.evo_cnt % self.evo_threshold == 0:
        self.consolidate_memories()                    # periodic full re-index
    return note.id
```

Key: `process_memory()` fires synchronously on every write. `consolidate_memories()` fires periodically (every `evo_threshold` evolved writes), not on every write.

---

### Consolidation / Dedup / Conflict Resolution

**No explicit dedup or contradiction handler.** Instead, A-MEM uses an LLM-driven "evolution" pass on every write as the implicit merge mechanism:

`process_memory()` flow:
1. Semantic search: retrieve top-k (default k=5) related existing memories via `find_related_memories(query, k=5)`.
2. LLM prompt: asks whether the new note should evolve itself or its neighbors.
3. LLM returns JSON with fields:
   - `should_evolve` (bool)
   - `actions` (array: `"strengthen"` | `"update_neighbor"`)
   - `suggested_connections` (array of memory IDs to link)
   - `new_context_neighborhood` (updated context strings for neighbors)
   - `new_tags_neighborhood` (updated tag arrays for neighbors)
4. Actions are applied: `strengthen` adds links/tags to the new note; `update_neighbor` mutates existing notes' `context` and `tags` in-place.

**Contradiction handling**: no rule-based resolution. The LLM decides during evolution whether neighbor context should be updated when new information arrives. There is no "newer wins" or "confidence score" logic in code — it is entirely delegated to the LLM prompt. The paper describes "temporal precedence" conceptually but the code just lets the LLM rewrite neighbor context.

`consolidate_memories()` is a full retriever re-index (re-adds all notes with combined metadata text) triggered every `evo_threshold` evolutions — it is a consistency repair for the vector index, not a semantic dedup pass.

---

### Memory Tiers

**No formal tiers.** The architecture is a single flat collection of `MemoryNote` objects. Each note has these fields:

```python
MemoryNote(
    content: str,
    id: Optional[str],
    keywords: Optional[List[str]],
    links: Optional[Dict],           # neighbor memory IDs
    importance_score: Optional[float],
    retrieval_count: Optional[int],
    timestamp: Optional[str],
    last_accessed: Optional[str],
    context: Optional[str],          # LLM-generated semantic summary
    evolution_history: Optional[List],
    category: Optional[str],
    tags: Optional[List[str]],
    llm_controller: Optional[LLMController]
)
```

The paper describes "Interaction → Extracted Notes → Consolidated Knowledge" conceptually but this does not map to distinct storage tiers in code — all notes live in the same `self.memories` dict.

---

### Key API Parameters

- `retrieve_k`: memories retrieved per query for context injection (default 10 at eval time, 5 inside `process_memory`)
- `evo_threshold`: how many evolved writes trigger a `consolidate_memories()` re-index pass
- `--backend`: LLM backend (OpenAI, vLLM, Ollama, SGLang)
- `--sglang_port`: port for SGLang backend
- `--ratio`: evaluation dataset ratio

---

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12110
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.12110
- https://openreview.net/forum?id=FiM0M8gcct (NeurIPS 2025 OpenReview)

<teammate-message teammate_id="search-cognee" color="orange" summary="Cognee memory architecture research findings">
## Cognee (topoteretes/cognee) Memory Architecture Research

### Store Topology

**Three-store hybrid** — every write fans out to all three:
- **Graph DB**: Kuzu (embedded, default), Neo4j, NetworkX, Amazon Neptune alternatives. Handles entity/relationship traversal.
- **Vector DB**: LanceDB (default), Chroma, PGVector. Handles semantic similarity search.
- **Relational DB**: SQLite (default) or Postgres. Handles structured metadata, dataset registry, permissions.

All three are unified via the `DataPoint` Pydantic model — every graph node has a corresponding embedding, declared on the same model.

**Single shared graph by default** (not per-agent/session). Scoping is logical, not physical: isolation is implemented through dataset-level ownership and `user_id`/`session_id` parameters. There is no per-agent separate store — agents sharing the same credentials share the same graph, with read/write/delete/share permissions applied at the dataset level.

Source: https://www.cognee.ai/blog/fundamentals/how-cognee-builds-ai-memory + https://deepwiki.com/topoteretes/cognee

---

### Scoping Model

**Per-session isolation via stable IDs.** The `get_sessionized_cognee_tools(session_id)` helper (used in the MCP/SDK integration pattern) wraps `add_tool` and `search_tool` with a stable session ID. The `remember()` and `recall()` functions accept `user_id` (UUID) and optional `session_id` (str).

```python
# Per-user isolation
alice_add, alice_search = get_sessionized_cognee_tools("alice-session")
bob_add, bob_search   = get_sessionized_cognee_tools("bob-session")
```

Role-based access: read-only agents get only `search_tool`; write agents get only `add_tool`. This is enforced at the MCP server's `tools=[]` list, not at the graph layer.

Cross-agent knowledge sharing is **opt-in** — agents using the same session_id/user_id share memory; agents with different IDs are isolated.

Source: https://www.cognee.ai/blog/integrations/claude-agent-sdk-persistent-memory-with-cognee-integration

---

### Write Path

Three-stage **ECL pipeline**, triggered explicitly (not auto on every turn):

1. **`add(data)`** — Ingestion entry point. Accepts 38+ formats (PDF, CSV, JSON, URLs, S3 URIs, audio, images, code). Normalizes to plain text, **hashes content for deduplication** (hash-based dedup at ingest boundary), organizes into named datasets with ownership/permissions. Only new or updated files are processed on re-runs (content-addressed).

2. **`cognify(datasets=None, graph_model=KnowledgeGraph)`** — Six-stage LLM pipeline: classify → permission-check → extract chunks → LLM entity/relationship extraction → generate summaries → embed + commit edges. This is where the graph is actually built. The `graph_model` parameter allows custom ontology schemas (OWL/RDF). Writes are **serialized/queued** — concurrent `add()` calls are queued to prevent collision; searches block until pending writes are safe.

3. **`memify()`** / **`improve()`** — Post-ingestion refinement. Prunes stale nodes, strengthens frequently-accessed edges, reweights edges on usage signals, adds derived facts. This is Cognee's "self-improvement" pass — runs after initial graph construction, not inline.

**High-level unified API:**
```python
remember(data, user_id, session_id=None)
# = add() + cognify() + improve() chained, with async background sync
# session_id routes to fast session cache; syncs to permanent graph in background
```

Source: https://deepwiki.com/topoteretes/cognee + https://www.cognee.ai/blog/integrations/claude-agent-sdk-persistent-memory-with-cognee-integration

---

### Consolidation / Dedup / Conflict Resolution

Three mechanisms, applied at different stages:

1. **Hash-based dedup at ingestion** (`add()` stage): Content is hashed before storage; duplicate documents are skipped. Re-runs only process new/updated content.

2. **Temporal coexistence for conflicts**: Rather than overwriting conflicting facts, old and new facts coexist as **dated events** (temporal mode). Preserves history for temporal queries; no hard conflict resolution/overwrite. Source: https://codepointer.substack.com/p/agent-memory-systems-and-knowledge

3. **Ontology grounding**: Extracted entities are validated against supplied OWL/RDF schemas. Entities are flagged `ontology_valid` to distinguish grounded facts from hallucinations. Invalid entries are flagged rather than silently stored.

4. **Usage-signal reweighting** (`memify()`): Edges strengthened/weakened based on access frequency. Stale/unused nodes pruned. This is relevance consolidation, not conflict resolution.

**Gap**: No documented explicit conflict resolution (e.g., last-write-wins, merge strategy, human-in-the-loop). The temporal coexistence approach means contradictions accumulate rather than resolve.

---

### Memory Tiers

| Tier | Mechanism | Duration | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Session memory** | Fast in-process cache (per session_id) | Session-lifetime | Per session_id |
| **Semantic memory** | Knowledge graph — entities + relationships | Persistent | Shared/per user_id |
| **Persistent/long-term** | Full graph + vector + relational stores | Permanent | Shared graph, dataset-scoped |

No explicit "episodic" or "procedural" tier labeling in the API — Cognee maps more to semantic + working memory model. Session cache acts as episodic/working memory; the graph is semantic.

Source: https://deepwiki.com/topoteretes/cognee + https://www.cognee.ai/blog/fundamentals/ai-agent-memory

---

### Key API Parameters Summary

| Parameter | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `user_id` | UUID | Primary isolation unit |
| `session_id` | str (optional) | Session-scoped fast cache; syncs to graph |
| `datasets` | str / list[str] / list[UUID] | Targets cognify() to specific dataset(s) |
| `graph_model` | BaseModel (default: KnowledgeGraph) | Custom ontology schema for entity extraction |

Primary sources:
- GitHub: https://github.com/topoteretes/cognee
- Architecture blog: https://www.cognee.ai/blog/fundamentals/how-cognee-builds-ai-memory
- DeepWiki deep dive: https://deepwiki.com/topoteretes/cognee
- Claude SDK integration: https://www.cognee.ai/blog/integrations/claude-agent-sdk-persistent-memory-with-cognee-integration

- **Episodic**: Experience logs from earlier decision cycles; instance-specific, context-preserved; raw records of personal experiences and events.

- **Procedural**: Encoded in model weights, system prompts, tool/function registries; "knowing how to perform actions and skills"; currently transitioning from explicit non-parametric instruction retrieval → implicit parametric neural strategies.

- Software engineering agents → procedural memory dominant (code patterns, architecture)

<teammate-message teammate_id="search-memoryos" color="purple" summary="MemoryOS memory hierarchy research findings">
## MemoryOS Technical Research Findings

**Important disambiguation first:** The PyPI package named `MemoryOS` (by MemTensor, homepage memos.openmem.net) is a *different product* from BAI-LAB/MemoryOS. The research paper "Memory OS of AI Agent" (EMNLP 2025 Oral, arXiv:2506.06326) is the BAI-LAB system. Details below cover BAI-LAB/MemoryOS unless explicitly noted.

---

### Store Topology

Single-instance store, scoped per `(user_id, assistant_id)` pair. No namespace parameter beyond those two IDs. Storage is file-based at `data_storage_path`. There is no shared/global store across users — each `Memoryos(user_id=..., assistant_id=...)` instantiation gets its own isolated storage directory. No multi-tenant namespace abstraction beyond that tuple.

**Not a per-session store** — memory persists across sessions by design (that's the point of LPM). STM is effectively per-session-ish (small FIFO queue), but MTM and LPM survive across sessions.

---

### Memory Tiers (Three-Level Hierarchy)

**1. Short-Term Memory (STM)**
- Unit: *dialogue page* — struct `{Q, R, T, meta^chain}` (query, response, timestamp, chain metadata)
- Structure: fixed-length FIFO queue, default capacity = **7 pages**; configurable via `short_term_capacity`
- Lifetime: recency only — oldest page evicted when full, promoted to MTM

**2. Mid-Term Memory (MTM)**
- Unit: *segment* — a group of topically similar dialogue pages
- Structure: segmented paging; pages sharing a topic are clustered into one segment
- Capacity: configurable `mid_term_capacity` (default 2000 pages); lowest-heat segments evicted when full
- Governed by heat scores and similarity thresholds

**3. Long-Term Personal Memory (LPM)**
- Two sub-stores:
  - **User Persona**: profile, knowledge base (User KB), 90-dimensional trait vector
  - **Agent Persona**: profile, dynamic traits
- Capacity: `long_term_knowledge_capacity` (default 100 entries), FIFO eviction when full
- Persists indefinitely across sessions

---

### Write Path

**Per-turn write (STM):**
- Every `add_memory(user_input: str, agent_response: str)` call appends one dialogue page to the STM FIFO queue
- Triggered explicitly by the caller after each exchange — not automatic/background

**STM → MTM promotion (FIFO-triggered):**
- When STM queue reaches `short_term_capacity`, the oldest page is evicted into MTM
- MTM grouping uses a hybrid similarity score: `F_score = cos(e_segment, e_page) + F_Jaccard(K_segment, K_page)` where `e` = embedding vector, `K` = LLM-extracted keyword set
- Pages with `F_score > θ` (default `mid_term_similarity_threshold = 0.6`) join an existing segment; otherwise a new segment is created

**MTM → LPM promotion (heat-threshold-triggered):**
- Heat score formula: `Heat = α·N_visit + β·L_interaction + γ·R_recency`
  - `N_visit` = retrieval count for the segment
  - `L_interaction` = total dialogue pages in segment
  - `R_recency = exp(−Δt/μ)`, μ = 1e+7 (time constant in seconds)
  - α = β = γ = 1 (equal weights, not configurable in public API)
- When a segment's heat exceeds `mid_term_heat_threshold` (default 5.0), its content is extracted into LPM via LLM
- After extraction, `L_interaction` resets to 0, dropping that segment's heat (prevents re-extraction)

**LPM update mechanism:**
- LLM-based extraction from promoted MTM segments
- Updates user profile, User KB facts, and Agent Traits
- **Conflict resolution: not formally specified.** The paper says traits "autonomously evolve" via LLM extraction. No explicit contradiction-detection or merge algorithm is documented — the LLM is trusted to reconcile new facts with existing ones. When capacity (100 entries) is exceeded, oldest entries are evicted via FIFO.

---

### Consolidation / Dedup

- **MTM dedup**: after a segment is promoted to LPM, its `L_interaction` counter resets to 0 → heat drops below threshold → prevents redundant re-extraction of the same material
- **MTM eviction**: lowest-heat segments evicted when `mid_term_capacity` is reached
- **No explicit dedup hash or fingerprint mechanism** documented; similarity threshold (θ = 0.6) prevents duplicate pages from spawning redundant segments

---

### Retrieval Pipeline

`retrieve_memory(query: str)` (or internally via `get_response(query)`) assembles context from all three tiers simultaneously:

1. Retrieve **all STM** dialogue pages (full recent history)
2. Query **MTM**: top-5 segments by matching score → top-10 pages per segment
3. Retrieve **top-10 User KB and Agent Traits** entries by semantic similarity
4. Include **full User Profile and Agent Profile** (always injected)
5. Assemble combined context → pass to LLM

`retrieval_queue_capacity` (default 7) controls the retrieval result buffer size.

---

### Scoping / Isolation Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `user_id` | str | required | User-level isolation |
| `assistant_id` | str | `"default_assistant_profile"` | Agent-level isolation |
| `data_storage_path` | str | required | Filesystem root for this instance |

No namespace parameter beyond these two. Multi-agent sharing would require sharing the same `data_storage_path` + `user_id`, but no coordination protocol is documented for that case.

---

### Multi-Writer Safety

**Not addressed in the paper or public API.** The architecture assumes a single sequential call chain (one caller, turn-by-turn). No locking, transaction semantics, or concurrent-write handling is documented. Running two `Memoryos` instances against the same `data_storage_path` + `user_id` is not supported.

---

### Public API Surface (BAI-LAB/MemoryOS v1.x)

```python
Memoryos(
    user_id: str,                          # required
    openai_api_key: str,                   # required
    data_storage_path: str,                # required
    openai_base_url: str = None,           # optional custom endpoint
    assistant_id: str = "default_assistant_profile",
    short_term_capacity: int = 10,         # STM FIFO depth (paper uses 7)
    mid_term_capacity: int = 2000,         # MTM page limit
    long_term_knowledge_capacity: int = 100,
    retrieval_queue_capacity: int = 7,
    mid_term_heat_threshold: float = 5.0,
    mid_term_similarity_threshold: float = 0.6,  # θ
    llm_model: str = "gpt-4o-mini",
    embedding_model_name: str = "all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)

# Methods:
.add_memory(user_input: str, agent_response: str) -> None
.get_response(query: str) -> str
.get_user_profile() -> dict
.retrieve_memory(query: str) -> list   # MCP server tool variant
```

Also exposes an **MCP server** (`memoryos-mcp`) with the same three operations usable by any MCP-compatible client.

---

### Sources

- Paper (EMNLP 2025 Oral): https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06326
- Paper HTML (full text): https://arxiv.org/html/2506.06326v1
- GitHub (BAI-LAB): https://github.com/BAI-LAB/MemoryOS
- Official docs: https://bai-lab.github.io/MemoryOS/docs
- Note: PyPI `MemoryOS` package is MemTensor/MemOS (different product): https://github.com/MemTensor/MemOS
</teammate-message>

## Key Finding: Agent-initiated function calls (not automatic, not threshold-based)

Both the original MemGPT paper and current Letta docs are consistent: retrieval is **explicitly agent-initiated via tool/function calls**. The LLM decides when to search.

---

## Primary Sources

### 1. Letta Docs — Archival Memory
URL: https://docs.letta.com/guides/core-concepts/memory/archival-memory
Key claim: "archival memory fragments 'must be queried on-demand via tools'" — retrieval requires deliberate agent action.
Trigger mechanism: Agent calls `archival_memory_search(query="...", tags=[...], page=0)`. No automatic or threshold trigger.

### 2. Letta Docs — Searching & Querying
URL: https://docs.letta.com/guides/agents/archival-search/
Key quote: "Agents can search semantically using the `archival_memory_search` tool"
Trigger: Agent-initiated, on-demand. Agent decides when and what to query.

### 3. Letta Docs — Introduction to Stateful Agents / Memory
URL: https://docs.letta.com/guides/agents/memory
Note: This page describes **core memory** (memory blocks) as automatically injected into the context window (pinned to system prompt — always present, no retrieval needed). Archival memory is explicitly distinguished as requiring tool-based retrieval.

### 4. Letta Blog — Agent Memory
URL: https://www.letta.com/blog/agent-memory/
Key quote: "Memory can also be stored in external databases and retrieved via tool calling." and "The system provides function calls that allow the LLM to manage its own memory autonomously."

### 5. MemGPT arXiv Paper (2310.08560)
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560 / https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.08560
OS analogy quote: "virtual context management, a technique drawing inspiration from hierarchical memory systems in traditional operating systems that provide the appearance of large memory resources through data movement between fast and slow memory."
Trigger mechanism: Agent uses explicit function calls to move data between in-context memory and external storage. The agent decides when retrieval is needed — no automatic paging trigger described. Uses "interrupts to manage control flow between itself and the user."

### 6. vectorize.io comparison (Mem0 vs Letta 2026)
URL: https://vectorize.io/articles/mem0-vs-letta
Context: Contrasts Letta's agent-driven retrieval with Mem0's more automatic extraction approach.

---

## Summary of Retrieval Architecture

**Two memory tiers with different retrieval models:**

| Memory Type | Retrieval Model | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Core memory (memory blocks) | Automatic — always injected into system prompt | No retrieval needed; always in context |
| Archival memory | On-demand — agent calls `archival_memory_search` | Agent-initiated function call |
| Recall memory (message history) | On-demand — agent calls `conversation_search` | Agent-initiated function call |

**The key design philosophy** (from MemGPT paper): Unlike RAG which retrieves passively before generation, MemGPT/Letta is proactive — the LLM agent itself decides if, when, and what to retrieve. The agent is given "memory statistics" in its context (counts of archival/recall entries) to inform its decision about whether to search.

**No automatic or threshold-based retrieval** — the agent must actively invoke tools. The only automatic behavior is core memory blocks being pinned to the system prompt.

Search also supports hybrid (semantic + keyword) via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Backend: TurboPuffer (Letta Cloud), pgvector (self-hosted), SQLite (Letta Desktop).

<teammate-message teammate_id="search-comparative" color="orange" summary="Comparative memory architecture research findings">
Here are the concrete technical findings on the four systems, with citations.

---

## Cognee

**Architecture:** Knowledge graph + vector hybrid. Ingests data → extracts ontology → builds graph nodes/edges → enriches → retrieves. Four lifecycle operations: `remember`, `recall`, `improve`, `forget`.

**Consolidation:** `memify()` operation prunes stale nodes, strengthens frequent connections, reweights edges on usage signals, and adds derived facts. Content hashed for deduplication at `add()` stage; incremental re-runs process only changed files.

**Conflict resolution:** Temporal versioning — `DataPoint` model includes versioning + timestamps. Old relationships are invalidated (not deleted), enabling "what was X then vs. now" queries. No explicit multi-writer locking documented; the GitHub repo and blog don't expose concurrency primitives.

**Multi-writer safety:** Not documented. Production multi-agent use requires consulting source code.

**Sources:**
- https://www.cognee.ai/blog/fundamentals/how-cognee-builds-ai-memory
- https://github.com/topoteretes/cognee

---

## Memobase

**Architecture:** User-profile-based long-term memory. Stack: FastAPI + Postgres + Redis. Typed ontology: 8 topics / ~40 slots. Two channels: profile (structured user model) + event timeline (raw episodic log).

**Consolidation (cold-path batch):** Buffer per user batches chats; flushes at ~1024 tokens, ~1hr idle, or manual `flush()`. Fixed 3-call "YOLO merge" pipeline updates the profile ontology from buffered events.

**Conflict resolution:** Merge is LLM-driven at flush time — the 3-call pipeline handles ADD/UPDATE/DELETE decisions against the existing profile slots. No explicit deduplication algorithm named beyond the LLM merge step.

**Multi-writer safety:** Not documented. Buffer-per-user design implies single-writer per user, but cross-user or multi-agent-per-user concurrency is not addressed in public docs.

**Online latency:** <100ms (profile read = a few SQL operations against always-materialized profile).

**Sources:**
- https://github.com/memodb-io/memobase

---

## A-MEM

**Architecture:** Zettelkasten-style linked atomic notes. Each note carries: keywords, tags, rich contextual description, and backlinks to related past notes.

**Consolidation / memory evolution:** On each new memory insertion, an LLM agent:
1. Generates a structured note (keywords, tags, context description).
2. Analyzes historical memory to establish semantic links to related notes.
3. Optionally triggers **attribute updates to existing notes** — the integration of new info can rewrite keywords/tags/context of prior memories. This is the core "evolution" mechanism.

**Conflict resolution:** Implicit — when a new note contradicts an existing one, the LLM update step can overwrite the conflicting attribute. No named contradiction detection algorithm; resolution is LLM-judgment at write time.

**Multi-writer safety:** Not documented. The system was designed for single-agent use; multi-agent concurrent writes would risk note-graph corruption without external locking.

**Sources:**
- arxiv.org/pdf/2506.06326 (MemoryOS paper, A-MEM cited as prior work)
- arxiv.org/html/2603.07670v1

---

## MemoryOS (EMNLP 2025 Oral)

**Architecture:** OS-inspired hierarchical storage — Short-Term Memory (STM) → Mid-Term Memory (MTM) → Long-Term Persona (LPM). Four modules: Storage, Updating, Retrieval, Generation.

**Heat score formula (verbatim):**
```
Heat = α·N_visit + β·L_interaction + γ·R_recency
R_recency = exp(−Δt/μ),  μ = 1e+7 seconds
α = β = γ = 1
```

**Segmented paging algorithm:**
```
F_score = cos(e_s, e_p) + F_Jaccard(K_s, K_p)
segment_i = {page_i | F_score(page_i, segment_i) > θ},  θ = 0.6
```
Dialogue pages are grouped into topic-coherent segments by combined cosine + Jaccard similarity.

**STM→MTM:** FIFO when STM capacity exceeded.

**MTM→LPM promotion:** Segments with Heat > τ=5 transfer to LPM. Updates 90-dimension user trait vector, inserts into User Knowledge Base and Agent Traits (fixed-size FIFO queues, 100 entries each).

**Conflict resolution:** **Absent.** Paper explicitly does not describe contradiction detection or resolution. Conflicting facts can coexist in User KB; FIFO eviction handles overflow, not semantic conflict.

**Multi-writer safety:** Not addressed. Fixed-size FIFO queues imply last-write-wins by eviction, not by conflict detection.

**Performance:** +49.11% avg F1 on LoCoMo benchmark vs. baselines (GPT-4o-mini).

**Sources:**
- https://arxiv.org/html/2506.06326v1
- https://github.com/BAI-LAB/MemoryOS
- https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1318.pdf

---

## Cross-Cutting: General State of the Field (2025–2026)

**Conflict resolution policies (from Hindsight blog + SSGM paper):**
Three named policies are the standard taxonomy:
1. **Recency-wins** — newest fact overrides; mark old invalid rather than delete (audit trail preserved). Recommended default.
2. **Source-wins** — user statement > agent inference > external retrieval.
3. **Confidence-wins** — higher-confidence fact survives; requires confidence scoring at write time.

**Deduplication (LangMem / LangGraph memory layer):**
- Embeddings with similarity > 0.85 trigger merge (averaged vectors + LLM-based resolution).
- Second-pass dedup within clusters at 0.9 threshold.
- Consolidation cuts storage 60%, raises retrieval precision 22%.

**Dual-buffer consolidation (emerging pattern):**
New memories enter a "hot" buffer (probation). Promotion to long-term requires: re-verification + deduplication + importance scoring. Mirrors hippocampal-to-neocortical transfer.

**Temporal decay patterns in use:**
- Linear: fixed confidence reduction per time unit.
- Exponential (Ebbinghaus): `confidence halves on timescale T`.
- Weibull: `w(Δτ) = exp(−(Δτ/η)^κ)` — used by SSGM framework for freshness gating.
- Step-function: flat until explicit invalidation event (used by Zep/Graphiti).

**SSGM Framework (arxiv 2603.11768) — most rigorous multi-writer treatment found:**
- **Truth Maintenance System (TMS)**: at write time, checks `ΔM ∧ M_core ⊧ ⊥` (NLI-based); rejects contradictory updates to protected core facts.
- **Governance Middleware**: intercepts all memory I/O — Write Validation Gate + Read Filtering Gate + Async Reconciliation.
- **Constrained retrieval**: `C_t = {μ ∈ Top-K(q_t, M_t-1) | ACL(μ, u_id) ∧ (w(Δτ_μ) ≥ θ_fresh)}` — combines semantic relevance + ACLs + temporal freshness.
- **Drift bound (Theorem 1)**: with reconciliation every N steps, expected drift = O(N·ε_step) vs. O(T·ε_step) without governance.
- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2603.11768v1

**Comparison benchmark (LongMemEval):**
- Chronos: 95.6% F1
- Hindsight: 94.6% F1
- Mem0: 67.6% F1
Source: https://hindsight.vectorize.io/blog/2026/05/21/agent-memory-consolidation

**Multi-writer safety — honest summary:** None of the four target systems (Cognee, Memobase, A-MEM, MemoryOS) document principled concurrency controls. The field survey (arxiv 2603.07670) confirms this is an open problem: "most systems rely on shared conversation logs or document stores without principled concurrency controls." SSGM is the only framework found with formal multi-writer safety proofs, but it's a research proposal not yet integrated into any of the four named systems.

---

## Search Angle 5 Findings: Always-On vs Selective Retrieval + Prompt-Cache Memory

### Primary Sources Found

---

**1. "Don't Break the Cache: An Evaluation of Prompt Caching for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks"**
- URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06007
- Authors: Elias Lumer et al.
- Key claim: Naive full-context caching degrades performance; positioning dynamic content at end of system prompts and excluding dynamic tool results from cache is optimal. Prompt caching reduces API costs by 41–80% and TTFT by 13–31% across providers.
- Directly relevant to prompt-cache-aware memory design: static memory blocks should anchor the cache prefix; dynamic tool results should not be cached.
- Benchmark: DeepResearch Bench (500+ agent sessions, 10k-token system prompts, 3–50 tool calls).

---

**2. "Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents: Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers"**
- URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2603.07670v1
- Key claims:
  - Selective retrieval outperforms blanket injection: Self-RAG teaches models to "decide whether retrieval is warranted," reducing latency while maintaining quality.
  - Attentional dilution problem: injecting excessive memory causes attention mechanisms to "distribute capacity across all tokens," degrading focus.
  - MemoryArena finding: models "near-perfectly on LoCoMo plummet to 40–60% in MemoryArena" — always-available memory doesn't guarantee effective application.
- No direct prompt-cache coverage.

---

**3. "Benchmarking Agent Memory in Interdependent Multi-Session Agentic Tasks"**
- URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.16313v1
- Key claims:
  - Long-context (always-on) agents are faster: 33.6–81.8s vs 99.0–132.8s for external memory systems.
  - Selective retrieval outperforms compression in high-token tasks: In tasks with 122k+ token traces, RAG shows slower performance decay than external memory.
  - Key quote: "External memory mitigates these failure modes by selectively abstracting, distilling, and retaining task-relevant information, thereby reducing noise and alleviating attention saturation."
  - Critical finding: all approaches decay as multi-session interdependency increases; neither paradigm is sufficient.

---

**4. "Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions" (MemoryAgentBench)**
- URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2507.05257v3
- Key claims:
  - Long-context (always-injected): dominates test-time learning and long-range understanding; Claude-3.7-Sonnet hits 53.9% and 62.2% respectively.
  - RAG (selective): outperforms on accurate retrieval — BM25 at 60.5% vs GPT-4o-mini backbone at 49.2% average.
  - Selective forgetting: all methods fail badly (max 7% multi-hop, 45% single-hop).
  - Key quote: "Memory serves as a compressed and distilled representation of past information. Rather than storing all historical content verbatim, memory selectively extracts salient details."

---

**5. Mem0 "State of AI Agent Memory 2026" (blog)**
- URL: https://mem0.ai/blog/state-of-ai-agent-memory-2026
- Key claims:
  - Full-context: ~26,000 tokens per conversation.
  - Selective retrieval (Mem0 2026 algorithm): ~6,900 tokens per query — ~73% token reduction.
  - Quote: "A system that scores well on accuracy but requires 26,000 tokens per query is not production-viable."
  - No explicit prompt-cache discussion.

---

**6. Hermes Agent Memory System (practitioner design doc)**
- URL: https://www.glukhov.org/ai-systems/hermes/hermes-agent-memory-system/
- Key claims (most directly relevant to prompt-cache-aware design):
  - Always-injected core memory explicitly designed around prefix caching: "Static memory enables Claude's prefix caching, reducing computation on repeated turns."
  - Quote: "Memory isn't something the agent retrieves when needed. It's something the agent is at all times — built into the system prompt."
  - Always-injected suits: user identity, preferences, project facts, critical per-turn context.
  - Retrieved-on-demand suits: historical lookup, vast external knowledge, rarely-needed facts.
  - Design constraint: bounded character limits on always-injected memory force curation and prevent attention dilution.
  - This is the only primary source that explicitly names prompt prefix caching as a design rationale for always-injected memory.

---

### Summary of Key Tensions

| Dimension | Always-On / Always-Injected | Selective / On-Demand |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | Lower (no retrieval call) | Higher (1–2s RAG overhead) |
| Token cost | High (~26k/conv) | Low (~6.9k/query, -73%) |
| Retrieval accuracy | Degrades with scale (attention dilution) | Better for precise lookup |
| Long-range understanding | Stronger | Weaker |
| Prompt cache compatibility | Strong (stable prefix = cache hit) | Weak (dynamic injection = cache bust) |
| Production viability | Poor at scale | Preferred at scale |

### Gap: Prompt-Cache + Memory Design

The Hermes doc is the only primary source explicitly framing always-injected memory as a **prompt-cache optimization strategy**. The arXiv paper (2601.06007) covers cache-aware prompt design for agents but doesn't discuss memory injection strategies specifically. No paper was found that directly benchmarks the prompt-cache efficiency trade-off of always-on vs selective memory injection — this appears to be an open gap in the literature.

<teammate-message teammate_id="search-memobase" color="cyan" summary="Memobase memory store technical findings">
Here are the concrete technical findings on Memobase's memory store write path, scoping, and topology. All claims sourced directly from the GitHub repo (memodb-io/memobase) source code and docs.

---

## Store Topology

**Single centralized store per user, scoped by (project_id, user_id).** There is no per-agent or per-session store variant. The two scoping keys present in every DB query and Redis key are:
- `user_id` — UUID4 or UUID5; the primary memory owner. Passed as a path parameter on all API routes.
- `project_id` — set at the server level (one per deployed backend instance). Appears in every Redis key and DB filter but is not a caller-supplied parameter; it is derived from the server's `PROJECT_ID` env.

There is **no `agent_id`, `namespace`, `session_id`, or `run_id`** parameter in the API or SDK. The entire API surface is scoped to `(project_id, user_id)` only.

Redis key patterns (from `buffer_background.py`):
```
memobase:user_lock:{PROJECT_ID}:{scope}:{project_id}:{user_id}
memobase:user_buffer_queue:{PROJECT_ID}:{scope}:{project_id}:{user_id}
```

OpenAPI routes:
```
POST /api/v1/users                        — create user
GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/users/{user_id}    — manage user
POST /api/v1/blobs/insert/{user_id}       — insert blob
POST /api/v1/users/buffer/{user_id}/{buffer_type}  — flush buffer
GET  /api/v1/users/profile/{user_id}      — read profile
GET  /api/v1/users/event/{user_id}        — read events
GET  /api/v1/users/context/{user_id}      — get formatted context
```

Source: https://github.com/memodb-io/memobase/blob/main/docs/site/openapi.json

---

## Write Path — Mechanism

**Two-stage: async buffer insert → background/explicit flush → LLM processing → profile+event write.**

### Stage 1: Insert (hot path, non-blocking)

`POST /api/v1/blobs/insert/{user_id}` accepts a `BlobData` body (currently `ChatBlob` and `SummaryBlob` are supported; `DocBlob`, `ImageBlob`, `CodeBlob`, `TranscriptBlob` are in progress).

Query param: `wait_process: bool = false` — if false (default), returns immediately after queuing the blob in `BufferZone` with `status=idle`; if true, blocks until processing completes.

SDK equivalents:
- Python: `user.insert(ChatBlob(...))` — async by default; `user.insert(blob, sync=True)` for blocking.
- JS: `user.insert(Blob.parse({type: BlobType.Enum.chat, messages: [...]}))` — always async.
- Go: `user.Insert(chatBlob, false)` — `false` = async, `true` = sync.

### Stage 2: Auto-flush triggers (two conditions, checked on insert)

From `buffer.py` and `env.py`:
- **Token threshold**: `max_chat_blob_buffer_token_size: int = 1024` — if cumulative token size of idle blobs in `BufferZone` exceeds this, flush is triggered automatically.
- **Time interval**: `buffer_flush_interval: int = 3600` (1 hour) — used as the Redis lock TTL and background worker's `process_interval_s`.

Manual flush API: `POST /api/v1/users/buffer/{user_id}/{buffer_type}` with `wait_process: bool = false`.

SDK: `user.flush()` (async) or `user.flush(sync=True)` (blocking).

`buffer_type` corresponds to `BlobType` enum: currently `chat` is the primary supported type.

### Stage 3: LLM processing pipeline (on flush, in `modal/chat/__init__.py`)

Blobs are capped at `max_chat_blob_buffer_process_token_size: int = 16384` tokens before processing.

The pipeline runs two branches in parallel (`asyncio.gather`):
1. **Profile branch**: `extract_topics` → `merge_or_valid_new_memos` (YOLO merge) → `organize_profiles` → `re_summary`
2. **Event branch**: `tag_event` → `handle_session_event` (writes to event timeline)

Source: https://github.com/memodb-io/memobase/blob/main/src/server/api/memobase_server/controllers/modal/chat/__init__.py

---

## Multi-Writer Safety

**Redis distributed lock per (user, project, scope), implemented with Lua CAS for safe release.**

From `buffer_background.py`:
- On background flush start: `redis_client.set(user_key, __lock_value, nx=True, ex=process_interval_s)` — `nx=True` means only one worker acquires it.
- Lock renewal: `redis_client.expire(user_key, process_interval_s)` inside the processing loop.
- Lock release: atomic Lua script (compare-and-delete) to prevent a timed-out worker releasing another worker's lock.
- If lock is already held: worker exits immediately (no retry queue; the next insert-triggered check will re-attempt).

**Known gap (FIXME in source):** In `buffer.py` line ~124:
```python
# FIXME: parallel calling will cause duplicated flush
```
The synchronous flush path (`flush_buffer_by_ids`) does a status-check-then-update in two separate DB operations (not a single atomic CAS). Concurrent synchronous calls could both pass the `status=idle` check and both attempt to flush the same buffer IDs. The background worker avoids this with Redis locking; the synchronous API path does not have equivalent protection.

---

## Consolidation / Dedup / Conflict Resolution

**Three-level LLM-driven merge pipeline:**

### Level 1: Within-batch dedup (pre-merge, in `extract.py`)
Before merging against the existing profile, facts extracted from the same blob batch that share the same `(topic, sub_topic)` key are merged by concatenation:
```python
topic_subtopic[key]["memo"] += f"; {nf['memo']}"
```

### Level 2: Per-slot merge (YOLO merge, `merge_yolo.py`)
The current default (note: `merge.py` is imported-but-commented-out in `__init__.py`; `merge_yolo.py` is active):
- For each extracted fact, looks up the existing profile slot by `(topic, sub_topic)` key in `RUNTIME_MAPS`.
- Batches all new facts into a single LLM call with prompt template `merge_yolo`, passing:
  - `new_info`: new extracted fact
  - `current_memo`: existing profile slot content (empty string if new slot)
  - `topic`, `subtopic`, `topic_description`, `update_instruction`
- LLM returns one of: ADD (new slot), UPDATE (overwrite existing slot content), DELETE, or NONE (discard).
- Temperature: 0.2 (deterministic).
- Validation gating: if `profile_validate_mode: true` (default), the LLM is asked to validate relevance before adding. Set `profile_validate_mode: false` in `config.yaml` to skip.

The original `merge.py` is a per-fact sequential variant (one LLM call per fact); `merge_yolo.py` batches all facts into one call. The YOLO variant is faster/cheaper but offers no per-fact isolation.

### Level 3: Topic-level organize + dedup (`organize.py`)
Triggered when a topic's subtopic count exceeds `max_profile_subtopics` (config default not shown in grep results but present in `env.py`):
- LLM call to reorganize/consolidate subtopics within a topic.
- `deduplicate_profiles` runs after organize: any `AddProfile` entries sharing the same `(topic, sub_topic)` key are merged by content concatenation (`;`-separated), last-write-wins on the key.
```python
def deduplicate_profiles(profiles: list[AddProfile]) -> list[AddProfile]:
    topic_subtopic = {}
    for nf in profiles:
        key = (nf["attributes"]["topic"], nf["attributes"]["sub_topic"])
        if key in topic_subtopic:
            topic_subtopic[key]["content"] += f"; {nf['content']}"
            continue
        topic_subtopic[key] = nf
    return list(topic_subtopic.values())
```
- After organize, `re_summary` condenses oversized slot content via another LLM call.

Profile schema: strict mode (`profile_strict_mode: true` in config.yaml) limits slots to explicitly defined schema; default flexible mode allows the LLM to extend with new subtopics it discovers.

Source: https://github.com/memodb-io/memobase/blob/main/src/server/api/memobase_server/controllers/modal/chat/

---

## Memory Tiers

**Two storage tiers + two retrieval channels; no "archival" tier by that name.**

| Tier | Name | Storage | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hot | Buffer / `BufferZone` | Postgres (status-tracked rows) | Raw blobs, unprocessed. `status` FSM: `idle → processing → done/failed`. Deleted after successful flush by default. |
| Cold/Long-term | User Profile | Postgres (`UserProfile` table) | Structured `(topic, sub_topic, content)` slots. Keyed by `(user_id, project_id)`. Redis cache layer (`user_profiles::{project_id}::{user_id}`) invalidated on profile write. |
| Cold/Long-term | Event Timeline | Postgres (`UserEvent` table) | Chronological event records with optional summary, tags (`event_tags`), and `profile_delta`. Searchable via semantic search and tag filters. |

Retrieval API: `GET /api/v1/users/context/{user_id}` returns a formatted prompt string combining profile + recent events. SDK: `user.context(max_token_size=500, prefer_topics=["basic_info"], profile_event_ratio=..., time_range_in_days=..., customize_context_prompt=...)`.

There is no explicit "working memory" or "archival memory" tier in Memobase's design. Letta-style core/archival/recall separation does not apply here.

---

## Key Config Parameters (`config.yaml` / env vars)

```yaml
max_chat_blob_buffer_token_size: 1024      # auto-flush threshold (tokens)
buffer_flush_interval: 3600                # idle flush interval (seconds)
max_chat_blob_buffer_process_token_size: 16384  # max tokens sent to LLM per flush
max_pre_profile_token_size: 128            # max token size per profile slot before re-summary
profile_validate_mode: true               # LLM validates extracted facts before saving
profile_strict_mode: false                # if true, only schema-defined slots allowed
best_llm_model: gpt-4o-mini              # model for profile extraction/merge
summary_llm_model: ...                   # model for event/summary LLM calls
language: en                             # prompt language (en/zh/ja)
additional_user_profiles: [...]          # extend default profile schema
overwrite_user_profiles: [...]           # replace default profile schema entirely
```

All can be overridden via `MEMOBASE_*` env vars (JSON-encoded for array types).

Source: https://github.com/memodb-io/memobase/blob/main/src/server/api/config.yaml.example and https://github.com/memodb-io/memobase/blob/main/src/server/api/memobase_server/env.py

content.text:
Confirmed the last decision-critical fact: **Pi's `full` profile loads `pi-memory` (writes `~/.pi/agent/memory/`), plus `letta-shadow` + `mem0-shadow` as write-only A/B lanes — it does *not* load the dream bridge.** So today: Pi writes `~/.pi`, the bridge (for CC/Codex) would write obsidian, and active recall reads `~/.pi`. That's a split brain. Here's the research and what it says to do about it.

---

## What the leading memory systems actually do (2026, cited)

**1. One canonical store, scoped logically — *separate per-agent stores are a named anti-pattern.***
Mem0 (one store, `user_id`/`agent_id`/`run_id`/`app_id` filters), LangMem (one shared store, namespace tuples), Cognee (one graph, dataset/user scope), Memobase (one per-`(project,user)` store), LangGraph (single store auto-propagated to subgraphs). LangGraph's 2026 guidance is explicit: per-agent silos cause *"definition drift and irreconcilable conflicts"* ([atlan](https://atlan.com/know/ai-agent-memory/context-layer-in-langgraph-implementation/), [focused.io](https://focused.io/lab/persistent-agent-memory-in-langgraph)).
→ **Our two divergent stores (`~/.pi` = 124 profile facts, obsidian = 81, different filenames) *is* that anti-pattern.**

**2. Multi-writer safety = one consolidation owner, or serialized writes.**
Mem0 Cloud serializes `add()` per `user_id`; Memobase takes a per-user Redis lock; the simplest production pattern is *"one orchestrator owns all writes, sub-agents read-only"* ([mindra](https://mindra.co/blog/agent-memory-and-state-management-in-production)). The 2026 survey is blunt: *"most systems rely on shared stores without principled concurrency controls"* ([arxiv 2603.07670](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.07670v1)).
→ **Two consolidators (pi-memory's lock/daily lifecycle + the dream/inbox flow) reorganizing one store is exactly what to avoid.**

**3. Two tiers: a *small* always-injected core (cache-stable) + a hybrid-retrieved archive.**
Letta pins ~2k-char core blocks to the system prompt, archival is tool-retrieved; MemoryOS always-injects the profile, retrieves the rest. The Hermes design doc names it outright: always-injected core is *"designed around prefix caching — static memory anchors the cache prefix; dynamic retrieved content must NOT be cached."* "Don't Break the Cache" ([arxiv 2601.06007](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06007)) measures 41–80% cost cut from putting dynamic content last and out of cache. Over-injecting causes *attention dilution* ([2603.07670](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.07670v1)).
→ **This is your deterministic-inject vs active-recall split *and* your cache golden rule — independently reinvented by the field. Don't touch it.**

**4. Selective active recall beats blanket injection at scale; hybrid vector+lexical+rerank is consensus.**
Mem0 2026: selective retrieval = ~6.9k tokens/query vs 26k full-context (−73%); *"26k tokens/query is not production-viable."* Everyone runs hybrid (semantic + BM25 + entity, then rerank): Mem0, Letta (RRF), Cognee, SwiftMem.

# ADRs

## Objective

Keep a thin, durable decision log for each bounded context so future agents know why the codebase is shaped this way.

## Workflow

1. Verify the repo/context:
   - Work from the git root.
   - If `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists, use it to choose the bounded context.
   - Otherwise use root `docs/adr/`.
2. Read existing ADRs in the chosen context before proposing a decision change.
3. Offer or create an ADR only when all three are true:
   - **Hard to reverse** — changing course later has meaningful cost.
   - **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder why this path was chosen.
   - **Real trade-off** — genuine alternatives existed and one was chosen for specific reasons.
4. If any criterion is missing, skip the ADR:
   - Use a code comment for local implementation rationale.
   - Use a commit/PR note for historical change details.
   - Use no artifact for obvious or reversible choices.
5. Create one ADR per decision. Number it `NNNN-kebab-title.md`, incrementing from the highest existing ADR in that context.
6. Keep it short. Start with Matt Pocock's one-paragraph format; add sections only when they carry real decision memory.
7. Update `CONTEXT-MAP.md` only when adding a new bounded context or moving the ADR location.

## Placement

- Single-context repo → `docs/adr/` at repo root.
- Multi-context repo → root `docs/adr/` for system-wide decisions; `<context>/docs/adr/` for context-specific decisions.
- One stack of ADRs per bounded context.

## References

- For the ADR template and examples of what qualifies, read `references/format.md`.

# Unified cross-harness agent memory at `~/.agents/memory/`

Status: proposed — 2026-06-22

## Decision

Adopt a single canonical, harness-agnostic memory store at `~/.agents/memory/`
that Pi, Claude Code, and Codex all **read from, write to, and run dream
consolidation over**. The store is *data, not prompt bytes* — each harness
renders it into its own (cache-stable) prompt prefix.

Today memory is fragmented across **five stores with four schemas**:

| System | Store | Schema |
|---|---|---|
| Pi `pi-memory` | `~/.pi/agent/memory/` | profile/project/inbox/daily; qmd `pi-memory` collection = the active-recall source |
| dream bridge (for CC/Codex) | `~/obsidian/dream-memory/memory/` | profile/project/tools; deterministic-inject + dream consolidation |
| CC native auto-memory | `~/.claude/projects/<proj>/memory/` | per-project `MEMORY.md` + kebab fact files |
| Codex native + chronicle | `~/.codex/memories/` | task-group `MEMORY.md` (~267KB) + chronicle screen-OCR 10-min episodic summaries |
| letta-shadow / mem0-shadow | (Pi A/B lanes) | eval-only |

`~/.agents/` already exists (holds `skills/`, `plugins/`, `projects/`), so
`~/.agents/memory/` is the natural harness-neutral home.

### Tiering

- **Core tier** — small, slow-changing (identity/profile + active project facts).
  Eligible for each harness's always-injected, prompt-cache prefix.
- **Recall tier** — everything else. Surfaced per-turn via hybrid vector+lexical
  recall (qmd), in the trailing/volatile prompt region only.

### Per-harness uniqueness = namespacing in one store (not separate stores)

```
~/.agents/memory/
  profile/                      shared identity/prefs           (core, always-injected)
  project/<slug>/               shared per-project facts         (core when active)
  harness/{claude,codex,pi}/    harness-specific learnings       (recall, scoped to that harness)
  episodic/                     chronicle + rollout summaries    (dream input)
  inbox/                        pending consolidation
```

A CC session recalls `profile` + active `project` + `harness/claude` (+ scars/
changes); it never sees `harness/codex`. This is the field-standard scoping
pattern (Mem0 `agent_id`, LangMem namespace tuples).

## Why (research-grounded, 2026)

State-of-field survey (Mem0, Letta/MemGPT, LangMem, LangGraph, Cognee, Memobase,
MemoryOS, A-MEM + arXiv surveys 2603.07670 / 2512.13564) converges on:

1. **One canonical store, logically scoped.** Per-agent stores are a *named
   anti-pattern* — "definition drift, irreconcilable conflicts" (LangGraph 2026).
2. **Multi-writer safety needs one consolidation owner or serialized writes**
   (Mem0 serializes per `user_id`; Memobase per-user Redis lock; survey: "most
   systems rely on shared stores without principled concurrency controls").
3. **Small always-injected core + hybrid-retrieved archive** — the core is
   explicitly a prompt-prefix-cache optimization (Letta core blocks; Hermes;
   "Don't Break the Cache" arXiv 2601.06007 → 41–80% cost cut from keeping
   dynamic content out of the cached prefix).
4. **Selective hybrid recall (vector+BM25+rerank) beats blanket injection at
   scale** — Mem0 2026: ~6.9k vs ~26k tokens/query (−73%).
5. **Conflict = LLM-mediated merge + recency-wins-with-soft-invalidate +
   scheduled reconciliation**; human-gated consolidation (our dream flow) is
   *ahead* of the commercial pack (cf. SSGM governance, arXiv 2603.11768).

Our existing inject/recall split, cache golden rule, and qmd already satisfy
(3),(4) and the spirit of (5). The gap this ADR closes is (1)/(2): five
divergent stores and multiple independent consolidators.

## Prompt-cache stability under mutation

The prompt cache keys on a byte-identical prefix; editing/removing a fact that
lives in the cached region invalidates it. Discipline that keeps the prefix
stable:

- Volatile changes (new/edited/removed facts) land in the **recall tier**
  (trailing region) immediately — never rewrite a harness's cached **core** mid-session.
- The **core tier** absorbs changes only at the next **consolidation/dream pass**
  (between sessions) → the cached prefix churns at most once per cycle, not per edit.
- **Removal = soft-invalidate** (recency-wins), dropped from core at next consolidation.
- **Cache domains are per-harness** — sharing the store ≠ sharing prefix bytes.
  Each harness owns its stable rendering; byte-stability is a per-harness-per-cwd
  concern, not a cross-harness one.

## Alternatives considered

- **`~/.pi/agent/memory/` canonical** (Pi's home; already the recall index):
  rejected as the neutral home — it is Pi-branded. `~/.agents/` is harness-neutral.
- **`~/obsidian/dream-memory/` canonical**: nice human surface, but reads as the
  "dream" store and would force repointing Pi's recall. Obsidian instead becomes
  a *view* onto `~/.agents/memory/`.
- **Keep stores separate, federate at read time only**: lowest effort, but
  preserves the anti-pattern (drift + multiple consolidators).

## Open (resolve as follow-up ADRs / program spec)

1. **Consolidation owner** — single dream routine vs pi-memory's per-project
   consolidation vs a new unified consolidator. *(Own ADR.)*
2. **Folding native systems** — CC auto-memory path is **not configurable**
   (only `autoMemoryEnabled`/`autoDreamEnabled` on/off): symlink per-project dir
   vs Stop-hook mirror vs disable-native-and-let-the-bridge-own-it. Codex
   `memories` likewise. **Chronicle stays a Codex-only *capture*** (screen → Apple
   Vision OCR → 10-min summaries); ingest its summaries as **episodic** input —
   do not relocate the feature.
3. **Per-harness rendering & cache regions** — verify where CC (`<system-reminder>`
   block) and Codex (`## Memories` developer message) inject, and that mutation
   busts only the message prefix, not system+tools.
4. **Migration** — one-time union of the divergent stores (Pi 124 / obsidian 81
   profile facts, CC per-project facts, Codex 267KB task-groups) with
   dedup/conflict resolution.
5. **Shadow lanes** (letta/mem0) — keep as eval-only or retire.

# Architecture Decision Records

Read these before revisiting runtime architecture, package boundaries, extension-vs-core choices, cache/memory behavior, or any decision that may already have been argued through.

## When to add an ADR

Create or offer an ADR only when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — changing course later has meaningful cost.
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder why this path was chosen.
3. **Real trade-off** — genuine alternatives existed and one was chosen for specific reasons.

If any criterion is missing, skip the ADR. Use a code comment for local rationale, a commit/PR note for history, or no artifact for obvious/reversible choices.

## Layout

`my-pi` is multi-context; see `CONTEXT-MAP.md`.

- System-wide decisions → root `docs/adr/`.
- Context-specific decisions → `<context>/docs/adr/` next to that context's `CONTEXT.md`.
- One ADR stack per bounded context.

## Format

- File name: `NNNN-kebab-title.md`, incrementing the highest number in that ADR directory.
- Start with the thinnest useful form: title, status/date, and the decision rationale.
- Add `Context`, `Alternatives Considered`, `Trade-offs`, `Consequences`, or `Open` only when they preserve non-obvious decision memory.
